title: Transitive vs. Intransitive Psychological Shifts (-ít vs. -ul/-ül)
goal: I can distinguish transitive psychological verbs (-ít / -tat) from their middle/intransitive counterparts (-ul/-ül, -ódik/-ődik, -szik)
I can pair animate experiencers correctly as accusative objects (felzaklat engem) or nominative subjects (elidegenedik, megnyugszik)
I can use B2 vocabulary of emotional turbulence, relief, and inner transformation

sections.title: Unit 11: The Unconscious, Dreams & Inner Conflict
body: Early twentieth-century Budapest was one of the world capitals of psychoanalysis and psychological fiction—home to Sándor Ferenczi's analytical circle as well as the introspective masterpieces of Milán Füst, Dezső Kosztolányi, and Mihály Babits. Hungarian is uniquely equipped to map subtle shifts of consciousness because its verb morphology systematically distinguishes external causation (-ít, -tat) from spontaneous inner transformation (-ul/-ül, -ódik/-ődik) and deliberate self-posturing (-kodik/-kedik/-ködik).

In this unit, you will master psychological valency pairs (megnyugtat vs. megnyugszik, felzaklat vs. felzaklatódik, elmélyít vs. elmélyül), behavioral -kodik/-kedik verbs, idiomatic case frames of inner conflict (szembenéz valamivel, belemerül valamibe), and the contrast between verbal suffixes and explicit reflexive pronouns (magát, magában, magával).
